## How a 63 year old’s marrow findings evolved into an urgent, high risk mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) diagnosis


### Presented by: Dr. Stephanie McAlhany, hematopathologist, Labcorp


## Key takeaways


- Bone marrow evaluation revealed MCL
- Labcorp’s Lymphoid Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) panel also referred to as comprehensive molecular sequencing, uncovered a TP53 mutation (VAF 12%), a molecular marker of ultra high risk disease
- Integrated molecular and morphologic testing guided the oncologist toward aggressive therapy and clinical trial consideration


## Early clinical presentation


Our patient, a 63 year old male, presented with pancytopenia. At first glance, his bone marrow biopsy showed 50–60% cellularity with a lymphoid infiltrate in a patchy interstitial and focal nodular pattern. Immunophenotyping confirmed MCL markers — CD20+, CD5+, Cyclin D1+, SOX11+. These findings suggested classic MCL, but the clinical picture was incomplete.


MCL is notorious for its variability. Some patients live years without therapy, while others face aggressive disease that demands immediate intervention.¹


## Diagnostic workup and findings


Flow cytometry confirmed a clonal B cell population with an immunophenotype consistent with MCL. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a complex karyotype, and FISH confirmed the hallmark CCND1::IGH translocation. These results established the diagnosis of MCL, but they did not yet explain the severity of the disease.


The turning point came with[Labcorp’s Lymphoid Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) panel](https://www.labcorp.com/content/labcorp/us/en/oncology/providers/testing-solutions/test-menu/heme-ngs-panels.html) . The test identified a TP53 mutation (c.880G>T, p.E294, VAF 12%). TP53 mutations occur in 14–31% of MCL patients and are recognized as independent predictors of ultra‑high‑risk disease.³ This single molecular finding shifted the patient’s risk profile dramatically.


“Risk stratification is critical. The TP53 mutation is the decisive marker that tells us when to escalate care” voiced the diagnostic expert.


## Escalation to high risk disease


Within days, a lymph node biopsy added another layer of urgency. Histology revealed blastoid morphology, an additional hallmark of aggressive disease.⁴,⁵ Ki 67 staining showed proliferation above 30%, and p53 immunohistochemistry demonstrated expression in more than 50% of cells.⁴


Taken together, these results — blastoid morphology, high Ki 67, and TP53 mutation, converged to classify the patient as ultra high risk MCL. What began as pancytopenia had become a diagnosis with profound therapeutic implications.


As Dr. Stephanie McAlhany, hematopathologist, Labcorp, rightly puts, *“MCL presents along a very broad spectrum of clinical behavior. Some patients on one end of the spectrum will essentially need no therapy initially, versus patients at the other end may actually initially go into a clinical trial and really need aggressive therapy from the beginning.* ”


## Why this matters


Risk stratification in MCL is not academic. It directly determines survival outcomes, therapy selection, and clinical trial eligibility.² Identifying TP53 mutations at diagnosis is critical, because they signal resistance to standard therapies and inferior outcomes.³


For this patient, the integration of NGS with cytogenetics and morphology provided actionable clarity. The oncologist could move beyond morphology alone and plan treatment that matched the gravity of the disease. In line with NCCN guidance, TP53 status became a decisive factor in therapy planning.²


## Impact on patient care


The oncologist now had the evidence needed to consider aggressive therapy or immediate clinical trial enrollment. Without NGS, the TP53 mutation would have remained hidden, and the patient might have been treated with standard regimens unlikely to succeed.³


By uncovering the mutation, the Lymphoid NGS panel connected diagnostic information directly to clinical decision making.⁶ The patient’s care plan could now reflect the reality of his disease, offering him the best chance at meaningful outcomes despite the poor prognosis associated with ultra high risk MCL.


## Implications for patient management


- NGS at diagnosis provides critical information, as TP53 status significantly influences prognosis and treatment planning in MCL³
- Morphology, proliferation index, and molecular markers together define disease aggressiveness ⁴,⁵
- Identifying ultra‑high‑risk disease early supports timely decisions on therapy selection and clinical trial enrollment ²
